text: Last lesson's charter named a scope. That scope creates a whole group of people with something at stake — and finding out who they are informally, by who shows up to meetings, is how programs get blindsided by objections after a policy is already written.

A thorough pass looks in four directions: data owners and stewards who have direct authority; the business units that consume the data even if they don't own it; IT, security, legal, and compliance, who weigh in on feasibility and risk; and leadership — the sponsor and council — plus any external regulators. The output is a stakeholder register.

Not every stakeholder needs the same attention. The power/interest grid plots each one by how much influence they have and how much they care. High power, high interest — manage closely. High power, low interest — keep satisfied. Low power, high interest — keep informed. Low power, low interest — just monitor.

The grid only matters if it changes what you do. For each stakeholder, decide how often they hear from the program, through what channel, and what you actually need from them — approval, input, or just awareness. A VP getting a generic monthly email when they could block the program is under-engaged; an analyst pulled into every steering meeting is over-engaged.
Next lesson: the standing body where the highest-power stakeholders actually do their work — governance councils in practice.
